faq.q: What is the normal PaCO₂ range?

faq.a: Yes, high FiO₂ can reduce hypoxic drive and worsen CO₂ retention
PaCO₂ >60 mmHg with pH <7.25 or patient is unresponsive

exam: A 68‑year‑old COPD patient presents with confusion and SpO₂ 88% on 4 L/min O₂. ABG shows PaCO₂ 68 mmHg, pH 7.22. — What is the next step? (Intubate and start mechanical ventilation; avoid high‑flow O₂)
A patient with asthma exacerbation has PaCO₂ 55 mmHg, pH 7.28. What does this indicate? — Respiratory acidosis; consider NIV if stable
A 45‑year‑old with pneumonia has PaCO₂ 48 mmHg, SpO₂ 92% on room air. What is the likely cause of hypercapnia? — Hypoventilation due to infection and reduced lung compliance
A patient on morphine shows low respiratory rate and PaCO₂ 60 mmHg. What is the management? — Reduce opioid dose or give naloxone; consider ventilation support
A 70‑year‑old with chronic heart failure has PaCO₂ 52 mmHg. What is the differential? — COPD, pulmonary edema, or neuromuscular weakness
A patient with severe sepsis has PaCO₂ 70 mmHg, pH 7.15. What is the priority? — Secure airway, start mechanical ventilation, treat sepsis
A 30‑year‑old with HIV presents with confusion and PaCO₂ 65 mmHg. What is a common tropical cause? — Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
ai.title: Hypercapnia
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Hypercapnia is excess arterial CO₂, often from hypoventilation. It presents with tachypnea, confusion, and cyanosis. Management focuses on treating the underlying cause and supporting ventilation.

b: Respiratory acidosis with normal or low pH
sections.p: Hypercapnia is defined as a PaCO₂ >45 mmHg. It results from impaired ventilation or increased CO₂ production. In low‑resource settings, common causes include COPD, asthma, pneumonia, and neuromuscular weakness.

t.b: Measures PaCO₂, pH, PaO₂ – confirms hypercapnia and acid–base status
Shows hypoxia; low SpO₂ may coexist with hypercapnia
Assesses lung pathology (COPD, pneumonia, pleural effusion)

sections.p: CO₂ is a respiratory waste product. The body maintains PaCO₂ via ventilation. Hypercapnia leads to respiratory acidosis, cerebral vasodilation, and impaired cardiac output.

t.b: Indicates severity of acidosis – <7.25 is severe
Primary marker of hypercapnia – >50 mmHg is moderate, >60 mmHg severe

sections.p: Patients may be confused, somnolent, or have a paradoxical tachycardia. In low‑resource hospitals, delayed recognition can lead to respiratory failure and death.

t.b: Look for accessory muscle use, nasal flaring, and paradoxical abdominal movement
Continuous CO₂ trend; rising values predict impending failure

sections.p: Examiners often ask about differential diagnosis, management steps, and interpretation of ABG. Focus on cause, severity, and urgent interventions.

t.b: PaCO₂ >60 mmHg with pH <7.25 – urgent intubation
Non‑invasive ventilation first if patient is stable; otherwise intubate

b: Treating only with oxygen – worsens CO₂ retention
sections.p: Assuming all hypoxia is due to low O₂; overlooking hypercapnia in COPD; misreading ABG pH; delaying intubation in severe cases.

t.b: Give low flow (≤4 L/min) to avoid CO₂ retention in COPD

sections.p: Treat underlying cause, support ventilation, and monitor ABG. In emergencies, secure airway and provide assisted ventilation.

t.b: Improves ventilation without intubation; use BiPAP or CPAP
Indicated when PaCO₂ >60 mmHg with pH <7.25 or patient is unresponsive

sections.p: Hypoventilation due to drug overdose, sleep apnea, or neuromuscular disease can mimic COPD. Respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation may mask hypercapnia.

t.b: Look for decreased consciousness and low respiratory rate

sections.p: Low PaO₂ may be normal in hypercapnic patients on high FiO₂; ABG pH can be misleading if metabolic alkalosis is present.

t.b: PaO₂ may appear normal; check PaCO₂

whenToSeekHelp: Severe confusion or loss of consciousness
